input: The Prandtl number is a dimensionless group of considerable importance in the study of heat transfer, and a clear understanding of its physical meaning is an essential foundation for its subsequent use. The Prandtl number is defined as the ratio of momentum diffusivity to thermal diffusivity, that is to say, it compares the rate at which momentum is transported through a fluid by viscous action with the rate at which heat is transported through the same fluid by conduction. When the value of the group is near 1, the two diffusivities are of comparable magnitude, and disturbances of velocity and of temperature spread through the fluid at broadly similar rates. When the value is large, on the other hand, momentum diffuses much more effectively than heat, and the region of fluid whose temperature has been affected by contact with a surface remains confined to a thin layer close to that surface, even though the influence of the surface on the velocity extends much further into the fluid. The group depends only on the properties of the fluid and on its state, and it provides a convenient means of judging, for any given fluid, the relative thicknesses of the layers within which velocity and temperature adjustments take place. It is for this reason that the group appears in the correlations by which surface heat transfer is calculated in practice across a wide range of equipment.
target: The Prandtl number sets two diffusivities side by side for the same fluid: the diffusivity of momentum, and the diffusivity of heat. The Prandtl number is defined as the ratio of momentum diffusivity to thermal diffusivity. Momentum diffusivity measures how fast a disturbance of velocity spreads through the fluid by viscosity alone; thermal diffusivity measures how fast a disturbance of temperature spreads by conduction alone. A value near 1 means the two spread at comparable rates. The velocity field and the temperature field then develop together: a layer of fluid that has been set in motion by a surface has been heated or cooled by that surface to a comparable depth, and neither field runs ahead of the other. A large value means momentum spreads far more readily than heat. The velocity disturbance reaches well beyond the region the temperature disturbance has reached, so the layer of fluid affected by a heated or cooled surface, in temperature, is thin compared with the layer affected in velocity. Heat then crosses a thin layer by conduction while momentum is exchanged across a much thicker one, and the surface heat transfer is governed by conduction across that thin layer. The number is a property of the fluid and its state, not of the apparatus: it is formed from the fluid's own transport properties, and it changes as those properties change with temperature. Its use is to say, for a given fluid, whether a surface process is limited by the spreading of momentum or by the spreading of heat, and the two limiting readings of the number frame every case between them.
